sceneHappening: Faith defined and illustrated: a long roll of those who trusted God before receiving what was promised
summary: "Now faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen. For by this, the elders obtained testimony. By faith, we understand that the universe has been framed by the word of God." Then a long series, each beginning "by faith": Abel offered a more excellent sacrifice and "through it he, being dead, still speaks"; Enoch was taken away, for "without faith it is impossible to be well pleasing to him, for he who comes to God must believe that he exists, and that he is a rewarder of those who seek him"; Noah prepared an ark; Abraham obeyed and went out "not knowing where he went," lived "as an alien in the land of promise" and "looked for the city which has the foundations, whose builder and maker is God"; Sarah received power to conceive; Abraham, tested, offered up Isaac, "concluding that God is able to raise up even from the dead." "These all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them and embraced them from afar, and having confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth... they desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed of them, to be called their God, for he has prepared a city for them." Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph acted by faith; Moses' parents hid him, and Moses refused to be called the son of Pharaoh's daughter, "choosing rather to share ill treatment with God's people than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a time, considering the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt." By faith they passed through the Red Sea, the walls of Jericho fell, and Rahab was spared. "What more shall I say? For the time would fail me if I told of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel, and the prophets, who through faith subdued kingdoms, worked out righteousness, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the power of fire... Others were tortured, not accepting their deliverance, that they might obtain a better resurrection. Others were tried by mocking and scourging... They were stoned. They were sawn apart... of whom the world was not worthy." "These all, having had testimony given to them through their faith, didn't receive the promise, God having provided some better thing concerning us, so that apart from us they should not be made perfect."
whySettingMatters: The roll call in chapter 11 is the best-known section of the letter, but it has a purpose: to show a long line of people who kept faith before the promise was fulfilled, so that the tired readers would continue. The definition in 11:1 uses two rare words: hypostasis ("assurance," or "substance") and elenchos ("proof," or "conviction"); translators have rendered it as "the substance of things hoped for" and "the evidence of things not seen," and both meanings are possible. Faith in this chapter is not a general mood but trust that God will keep a promise that has not yet come. The pattern also includes a paradox: some by faith win victories (11:33-35a) while others by faith are tortured and killed (11:35b-38), and both are commended. The mention of "sawn apart" may refer to a tradition about the prophet Isaiah. "The reproach of Christ" borne by Moses (11:26) reads the Old Testament in light of Christ; the writer sees the earlier faithful as sharing in the same story. The last verses say that these people have not yet "received the promise," so that they are made perfect together with the readers; the promise is not complete without the whole people of God. The list contains some surprising names (Rahab, a Canaanite woman who sheltered spies; Samson; Jephthah), a sign that faith, not moral record, is the point.

people.note: Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Rahab, and many unnamed others.
Went out not knowing where, lived in tents, and offered Isaac.
Chose to share ill treatment with God's people over the treasures of Egypt.
Told that the faithful of old need them to be made perfect together.

questions: "Faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen." How would you put that in your own words?
Some of the people in the list win and some are killed, and all are commended. What does that say about what faith is for?
"They desire a better country, that is, a heavenly one." How does the pilgrim image change how you hold things?
"Apart from us they should not be made perfect." What does it mean that those who came before are waiting for the whole people of God?
